content: Discussion thread for #Project announcements > Software Foundations in Lean: Call for Contributions

This is very exciting so definitely looking forward to reading it.

Just in case it's helpful, your link (http://softwarefoundations.org/) will raise an error for anyone with HTTPS required in their browser (which is generally a good idea in 202X) because you have a redirect set up to https://softwarefoundations.cis.upenn.edu/ but only via HTTP.

I have been writing a counterpart on my own. You can look at my draft book or the GitHub repo (maybe the name is too ambitious).

My motivation is that the official Lean tutorials are not the way I learned type theory, and I am interested in making a (toy) Lean in Lean itself (so that I know how to make a cubical version). So I plan to write the following:

  • Logic in Lean: this is a bit like the first volume of SF, but I will put the proof of Kripke semantics of intuitionistic logic (see here).

  • Computation models:
    I plan to first introduce partial recursive functions as the most naive model of computation. Next,
    I will discuss lambda-calculus and prove the normalization of STLC with presheaf semantics.
    Then, I will discuss Turing machine and language Imp and Hoare Logic.
    Finally, I will introduce how IO is implemented and what is Monad.
    Maybe Halting problem and Godel's incompleteness theorem should also be mentioned.

  • Type theory: A translation of this in Lean.

  • Toy Lean: make the toy Lean, its parser and compiler (maybe the cubical version).
  • Silicon: Coq also have a hardware design DSL called KoiKa.
    I am not satisfied with HDLs such as verilog. It is easy to make a code generator in Lean so I don't have
    to suffer verilog. Then, why don't we further model a digital circuit and verify its correctness?

What I have done is most of the volume Logic in Lean (check my draft) and a tool just like coqdoc that could build a Lean project into a book-like website. (The tool is written in a dirty way with python. I think it is better to write it in Lean since the parser has already been there, but I don't know how).

To be frank, SF is the book I was reading when learning how to use a proof assistant. I really hope a counterpart in Lean. I intend to introduce more Lean-idiomatic things in my book. Also, I think some parts of SF are not of my taste. For example, the proof of normalization is a bit ad-hoc. This proof comes from normalization by evaluation (NBE). (I made a draft implementation of NBE). I also expect a formalization of CIC gradually evolved from STLC. This is why I plan to write my book quite different from SF.

What's your idea on that?
